source_text: The Fairview Housing Authority's own unit-status ledger, released under a records request in March, shows that of the 214 wheelchair-accessible apartments the authority reports to the state as part of its accessible-housing inventory, 61 have carried the internal code "Priority B — Temporary Hold" continuously since at least January 2022. The ledger defines Priority B as a status assigned for the duration of a unit inspection or repair, not to exceed 45 days, but the authority's own maintenance records show only 9 of the 61 units under Priority B have had any inspection or repair logged in the past two years. A tenant named Marcus Oyelaran, who has used the waitlist since 2021, told the authority's oversight board in February that he had called about a Priority B unit on Delancey Street four separate times since 2022 and been told each time that the unit was temporarily unavailable, not for the waitlist. The board's own annual compliance report, filed with the state in December, lists all 214 units as available accessible inventory without mentioning Priority B at all. When the state auditor's office asked, in a letter dated January 14, why the vacancy rate for accessible units appeared to be zero for three consecutive years despite an average 18-month waitlist, the authority's written response, dated January 29, stated that units under administrative hold are counted as occupied for reporting purposes, consistent with standard practice, a sentence that does not appear in any written policy the authority has published. No document reviewed states who first proposed treating Priority B units as occupied for state reporting, or when that practice began.

commission_brief.hidden_mechanism: A status created to describe a brief administrative pause is, through indefinite renewal and a reporting rule that counts it as occupancy, converted into a permanent removal from the accessible-unit waitlist without that removal ever being recorded as one.
commission_brief.why_disability_knowledge_changes_subject: Knowing how waitlists are actually audited -- by point-in-time occupancy snapshots, not by how long any single unit has sat in a holding status -- reveals why 'for the duration of a unit inspection or repair, not to exceed 45 days' can be renewed indefinitely without a single day of it ever being individually false.
